text: The Yasa was the body of law and decrees attributed to Genghis Khan, governing military discipline, administration and social conduct among the Mongols. Mongol imperial governance rested on it. The Chagatai Empire and the Ilkhanate both upheld the Yasa, and tensions between it and Islamic law arose as their rulers converted to Islam.

The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, flowing from the Tibetan plateau across the north China plain to the Bohai Sea. Chinese civilisation is considered to have begun along it, but it is notorious for devastating floods and changes of course. Accounts of the Gokturk Empire note that Qapaghan Qaghan crossed it repeatedly in raids on Tang China, and its floods of 1344 contributed to the decline of the Yuan Dynasty.

The Yongzheng Emperor was the third Qing emperor to rule China, reigning from 1722 to 1735 between the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors. He strengthened central administration, created the Grand Council and reformed taxation, curbing corruption among officials. Accounts of the Qing Empire describe his tax reforms of the 1720s as important to the empire's economy and governance.

The Zanata were one of the major Berber confederations of North Africa, many of them pastoral nomads of the Maghreb and the northern Sahara. They were prominent in the politics of the medieval Maghreb, later founding the Marinid and Zayyanid dynasties. Accounts of the Ghana Empire record that Ghana captured the trans-Saharan oasis city of Awdaghast from Zanata Berbers in 992 CE.

Zeng Guofan was a Chinese scholar-official and military leader who raised and commanded the Xiang Army, which was central to the suppression of the Taiping Rebellion. He was also a leading figure in the Self-Strengthening Movement. The success of such Han Chinese regional armies transferred real military power away from the Manchu court.

Ashurnasirpal II was King of Assyria from 883 to 859 BCE and one of the founders of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. In yearly campaigns he subdued the Aramaean states along the Euphrates and the Khabur and the highlands of Nairi and Zamua, and reached the Mediterranean, collecting tribute from Patina and the Phoenician cities. His inscriptions boast of brutal punishment of rebels. He rebuilt Kalhu, modern Nimrud, as his capital.

Juan Manuel de Rosas was a rancher and Federalist caudillo who governed Buenos Aires from 1829 to 1832 and from 1835 to 1852 with extraordinary powers, directing the foreign affairs of the Argentine Confederation. He dealt with frontier peoples through campaigns, treaties and rations, persecuted opponents through the Mazorca and resisted French and British blockades. Defeated by Justo José de Urquiza at Caseros in 1852, he died in exile in England.

Neferhotep III was a king of the Theban Sixteenth Dynasty of Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period, when the Hyksos ruled the north. He is one of the better-attested rulers of the dynasty: a stela from his reign boasts that he rescued Thebes in a time of hunger and war.

Benjamin Kállay was a Hungarian statesman and historian who served as joint finance minister of Austria-Hungary from 1882 to 1903, in charge of the administration of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He promoted a shared Bosnian identity to counter Serbian and Croatian nationalism and developed railways, mines, forestry and schools. His rule shaped Sarajevo's architecture and institutions.

Henry III, Margrave of Meissen, called the Illustrious, was a Wettin prince who ruled Meissen from 1221. Through his mother, a Ludowingian, he claimed Thuringia after the death of Henry Raspe and won it in the War of the Thuringian Succession by 1264. He was also a Minnesinger and patron of court culture, and his gains made the Wettins one of the leading houses of the empire.

The Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany (USPD) was formed in 1917 by socialists who broke with the Social Democrats over support for the First World War. It was prominent in the revolution of 1918–1919 and in council governments such as that of Bremen. In 1920 most of its members joined the Communists, and the rest rejoined the Social Democrats in 1922.

Silko was a king of Nobadia in Lower Nubia known from a Greek inscription in the temple at Kalabsha. In it he calls himself king of the Nobadae and all the Ethiopians and boasts of repeated victories over the Blemmyes, whom he drove from the Nile valley. The text is a key source for the rise of Nobadia shortly before its conversion to Christianity.

Monte Cassino is a hill above Cassino in southern Italy where Benedict of Nursia founded his monastery around 529, from which the Benedictine order grew. Sacked by the Lombards around 577 and by Arab raiders in 883, it was rebuilt and became a great centre of learning and manuscript copying, closely linked with the Lombard principalities of Benevento and Capua. The abbey was destroyed by Allied bombing in 1944 and rebuilt.

The Orkhon River flows through central Mongolia into the Selenga, and its valley was the political heart of successive steppe empires. The Second Turkic Khaganate raised its memorial stelae, the Orkhon inscriptions, there in the 8th century, and the Uyghurs built their capital Ordu-Baliq on its banks. The Mongols later founded Karakorum in the same valley, now a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape.

Shaykh Uways was sultan of the Jalayirid dynasty from 1356 to 1374, son of its founder Hasan Buzurg. He took Tabriz in 1360 and ruled both Iraq and Azerbaijan, the height of Jalayirid power. Presenting himself as heir to the Ilkhans, he was a patron of Persian poetry and painting, and his court at Baghdad and Tabriz encouraged manuscript illustration.

Shimazu Nariakira was daimyo of the Satsuma Domain from 1851 to 1858 and one of the most forward-looking lords of late Tokugawa Japan. He built Western-style reverberatory furnaces, shipyards, glassworks and factories at the Shuseikan in Kagoshima, and promoted able retainers such as Saigo Takamori. His modernisation prepared Satsuma to become one of the leaders of the Meiji Restoration.

Siemowit III of Masovia was a Piast duke who reunited most of Masovia in the 1370s after the deaths of his relatives. A vassal of the Polish Crown, he issued a law code for the duchy and promoted its towns. After his death the lands were again divided among his heirs.

The Tel Dan stele is a fragmentary Aramaic inscription of the 9th century BCE found in 1993–1994 at Tel Dan in northern Israel. Probably set up by Hazael of Aram-Damascus, it boasts of victories over a king of Israel and a king of the 'House of David', the earliest widely accepted reference outside the Bible to David's dynasty.

The War of the Thuringian Succession of 1247–1264 followed the death without heirs of Henry Raspe, the last Ludowingian landgrave of Thuringia. Henry the Illustrious, Margrave of Meissen, fought Sophie of Brabant, daughter of Landgrave Louis IV, for the inheritance. The settlement gave Thuringia to the Wettins of Meissen, while Sophie's son Henry I kept the western lands as the new Landgraviate of Hesse.

Tōdō Takatora (1556–1630) was a Japanese warlord who served several masters, including Toyotomi Hideyoshi, before siding with Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara in 1600. Known as a castle builder, he worked on Edo, Osaka and Nijō castles. In 1608 he received the Tsu domain in Ise and Iga provinces, which his descendants held until 1871.

Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628–1701) was the second lord of the Mito domain and a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu. He began the compilation of the Dai Nihonshi, a vast history of Japan, which encouraged the Mito school of learning with its emphasis on loyalty to the emperor. He is popularly known as Mito Kōmon, hero of a long-running television drama.

The Gonbad-e Sorkh, or Red Dome, is a brick tomb tower built in 1147–48 in Maragheh, north-western Iran, under the Ahmadili rulers. Square in plan, with a domed chamber above a crypt, it is decorated with patterned brickwork and touches of glazed tile. Maragheh has several other medieval tomb towers of the Seljuk and Mongol periods.

Angers is a city on the Maine river near the Loire in western France, the historic capital of Anjou. As Juliomagus it was the chief town of the Gallic Andecavi under Rome, later taking their name. It was the seat of the counts of Anjou, whose line produced the Plantagenet kings of England, and its 13th-century castle houses the Apocalypse Tapestry.

The Abam are an Igbo clan of modern Abia State in south-eastern Nigeria. Known as warriors, they served the Aro Confederacy as mercenaries in the 18th and 19th centuries, raiding communities that defied Aro authority and helping to supply captives for the slave trade. Their martial traditions survive in dances and ceremonies.

Lancia was the chief stronghold of the Astures on the plain of the river Esla, near modern León in north-western Spain. Roman historians record that the legate Titus Carisius besieged and took it during the Cantabrian Wars around 25 BCE, sparing the town so that it would be a monument to his victory. Excavations at Villasabariego have uncovered remains of the later Roman settlement.

Arras is a city in the Pas-de-Calais department of northern France and the historic capital of Artois. It began as Nemetocenna, the chief town of the Gallic Atrebates, whose name survives in Arras and Artois. In the Middle Ages it grew rich on wool and tapestry weaving, so that 'arras' became an English word for tapestry, and it gave its name to the Union of Arras of 1579.

Gunung Kawi is an 11th-century temple complex at Tampaksiring, Bali, where ten shrine facades about seven metres high are carved into cliffs on both sides of the Pakerisan river. They are traditionally held to be memorials to King Anak Wungsu and members of his family. The site is part of Bali's UNESCO-listed cultural landscape.

Beauvais is a city in northern France, capital of the Oise department in Hauts-de-France. It grew from Caesaromagus, the Roman chief town of the Bellovaci, and became a bishopric. Its Gothic cathedral of Saint-Pierre has the highest choir vault in the world, which partly collapsed in 1284, and its tapestry manufactory was founded in 1664.

The Kayan are an Indigenous Dayak people of Borneo, living along the upper reaches of rivers such as the Kayan in North Kalimantan, the Mahakam in East Kalimantan and the Baram and Rajang in Sarawak. They were traditionally rice farmers living in longhouses under a hereditary aristocracy, and were known as warriors and craftsmen. A Kayan chiefdom was the origin of the ruling house of the Bulungan Sultanate.

Nonantola Abbey is a Benedictine monastery near Modena in northern Italy, founded in 752 by Anselm, a former Duke of Friuli and brother-in-law of the Lombard king Aistulf. Favoured by Lombard and Carolingian rulers, it grew into one of the richest abbeys of Italy, with a well-known scriptorium. Its Romanesque church dates from the 12th century.

Cayuga Lake is the longest of the Finger Lakes of central New York, about 61 km long, with the city of Ithaca at its southern end. It lay in the centre of the homeland of the Cayuga, one of the five original nations of the Iroquois Confederacy, who lived in villages along its shores until the American Revolutionary War. The lake drains north towards Lake Ontario.

The Dilwara Temples are a group of five Jain temples at Mount Abu in Rajasthan, India, famed for their carved white marble interiors. The oldest, the Vimal Vasahi dedicated to Rishabhanatha, was built in 1031 by Vimala, a minister of the Chaulukya king Bhima I, and the Luna Vasahi was added in 1230 by the brothers Vastupala and Tejapala.

The Lanzón is a carved granite monolith about 4.5 metres tall standing in the centre of the Old Temple at Chavín de Huántar in the Peruvian Andes. Shaped like a lance, it depicts a fanged deity with claws and snake-like hair and was the chief cult image of the Chavín culture, set in a narrow cross-shaped gallery deep within the temple.

Murata Seifū (1783–1855) was a samurai official of the Chōshū domain who led its Tenpō-era reforms from 1838. He reduced the domain's heavy debts, cut spending and encouraged and regulated the production of paper, salt and wax, while developing trade through the port of Shimonoseki. His reforms strengthened Chōshū's finances before the domain became one of the leaders of the Meiji Restoration.

The River Feale rises in the Mullaghareirk Mountains near the borders of Cork and Limerick and flows north-west through north Kerry, past Listowel, to the Shannon estuary near Ballybunion, Ireland. Part of its course forms the border between counties Limerick and Kerry. Its valley lay in the centre of the territory of the Ciarraige Luachra in the early Middle Ages.

The Barbados Slave Code of 1661, formally An Act for the better ordering and governing of Negroes, was a law passed by the colonial assembly of Barbados to regulate enslaved Africans. It treated the enslaved as property, imposed harsh punishments and gave masters broad powers with few protections. Slave codes in Jamaica, South Carolina, Antigua and other English colonies were modelled on it.

Sydney Cove is a small bay on the southern shore of Port Jackson, in the centre of modern Sydney, Australia. The First Fleet under Arthur Phillip landed there on 26 January 1788 to found a penal colony, the first British settlement in Australia, an event marked as Australia Day. Its shores are now occupied by Circular Quay, the Sydney Opera House and The Rocks.

The Palazzo dei Priori is the town hall of Volterra in Tuscany, built from 1208 to 1257 and considered the oldest surviving town hall in Tuscany. Its stone façade, decorated with the coats of arms of Florentine governors, was the model for the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. It is still the seat of the town council.

Bruges is a city in West Flanders, Belgium, linked to the North Sea by canals. From the 12th to the 15th century it was the commercial capital of north-western Europe, home of a Hanseatic office and Italian banking houses, a leading centre of the Flemish cloth trade and of painters such as Jan van Eyck. The silting of its waterway shifted trade to Antwerp, leaving a well-preserved medieval centre.

The Aargau is a region of northern Switzerland on the lower Aare, Reuss and Limmat, today a canton with its capital at Aarau. It was the homeland of the Habsburg dynasty, whose ancestral castle stands near Brugg, until the Swiss Confederates, led by Bern, conquered it in 1415. Ruled for centuries as subject land of Bern and of the Confederates in common, it became a full canton under Napoleon's Act of Mediation in 1803.

Wolfenbüttel is a town in Lower Saxony, Germany, on the Oker south of Brunswick. From the 15th century until 1753 it was the residence of the dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, who built a large palace and the Herzog August Library, one of the best-known early modern libraries in Europe. Gotthold Ephraim Lessing worked there as librarian from 1770.

Charroux is a village in the Vienne department of western France that grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in the late 8th century and known for its relics. A church council held there in 989 issued the first known decrees of the Peace of God. In the 10th century its lords, beginning with Boso the Old, became counts of La Marche.

Sophie of Brabant (1224–1275) was a daughter of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary and Landgrave Louis IV of Thuringia, and the wife of Duke Henry II of Brabant. When the Ludowingian line died out in 1247 she claimed the Thuringian inheritance for her son Henry and fought the Wettin margrave Henry the Illustrious in the War of the Thuringian Succession. The 1264 settlement gave Hesse to her son, Henry I, the first Landgrave of Hesse.

Tremp is a town in the province of Lleida, Catalonia, capital of the Pallars Jussà district on the Noguera Pallaresa. In the Middle Ages it lay in the centre of the county of Pallars Jussà, in a basin of farmland ringed by castles. Today it is a market town known for the nearby reservoirs and the dinosaur fossil sites of the Tremp basin.

Krak des Chevaliers is a Crusader castle in western Syria, on a hill commanding the Homs Gap between the coast and the interior. The Count of Tripoli granted it to the Knights Hospitaller in 1142, and they rebuilt it into one of the strongest fortresses of the Middle Ages. It fell to the Mamluk sultan Baybars in 1271 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Wolfegg is a municipality in Upper Swabia, in the Ravensburg district of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Its Renaissance castle has been the seat of the Waldburg-Wolfegg line since the 16th century and housed a well-known art collection, including the late-medieval Wolfegg Housebook. Martin Waldseemüller's world map of 1507, the first to use the name America, was rediscovered in the castle in 1901.

The Shandwick Stone, or Clach a' Charridh, is a Pictish cross-slab of around 800 CE standing above the village of Shandwick in Easter Ross, Scotland. One side carries a large cross with raised bosses, the other Pictish symbols, a hunting scene and a panel of spiral ornament. It is now protected inside a glass enclosure.

Anum-muttabbil was a ruler of the Mesopotamian city of Der, east of the Tigris, around the start of the 2nd millennium BCE. In an inscription he claimed to have struck down the heads of Anshan, Elam and Shimashki, a boast that shows Der acting as an independent power on the Elamite frontier after the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur.

Kalkar is a town on the lower Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, founded by the counts of Cleves in 1230. It prospered from the cloth trade in the late Middle Ages, when its church of St Nicolai was furnished with carved altarpieces by a school of local woodcarvers. It is also known for a nuclear power station that was completed but never operated and is now an amusement park.

Eberhard I, called the Illustrious, was Count of Württemberg from 1279 to 1325. He fought the kings of Germany and the Swabian imperial cities, and lost most of his lands in 1312 to forces acting for Emperor Henry VII, but recovered them after the emperor's death. He made Stuttgart the residence of the counts.

Ludovico Antonio Muratori (1672–1750) was an Italian priest and historian, librarian of the Este dukes in Modena from 1700. His Rerum Italicarum Scriptores collected the sources of medieval Italian history and became the basis of its critical study. He also discovered the Muratorian fragment, the oldest known list of books of the New Testament.

Otto II, called the Illustrious, was a Wittelsbach Duke of Bavaria from 1231 to 1253 and, through his marriage to Agnes of the Palatinate, Count Palatine of the Rhine from 1228. He supported the Hohenstaufen emperors against the papacy and was excommunicated. On his death his sons Louis II and Henry XIII divided the duchy in 1255, the first of many Wittelsbach partitions.

The Holy Robe is a relic kept in Trier Cathedral and venerated as the seamless tunic worn by Jesus before the crucifixion. Tradition says Empress Helena sent it to Trier; it is first clearly documented in the 12th century and was first shown publicly to pilgrims in 1512. Later exhibitions, as in 1844 and 1996, drew hundreds of thousands of pilgrims.

The Sittaung is a river of central and southern Myanmar, flowing south for about 420 km between the Bago Yoma hills and the Shan Plateau into the Gulf of Martaban. The town of Toungoo on its middle course was where the Toungoo dynasty arose. In February 1942 British and Indian troops retreating from the Japanese suffered heavy losses when the Sittang bridge was blown up with many of them still on the far bank.

Benelux is the union of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. It began as a customs union agreed by their governments in exile in London in 1944 and in force from 1948, and became an economic union by a treaty of 1958 that took effect in 1960. Its close cooperation was a model for the European Communities, which all three countries co-founded.

The Moscow Kremlin is the fortified complex in the centre of Moscow, on a hill above the Moskva river. From the fourteenth century it was the seat of the grand princes of Moscow and later of the tsars, and under Ivan III Italian architects rebuilt its brick walls, towers and cathedrals in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. It is the official residence of the President of Russia.

Blaj is a small town in Alba County, Romania, in central Transylvania. It became the seat of the Romanian Greek Catholic Church after the union of many Orthodox Romanians with Rome around 1700, and its schools, opened in 1754, made it one of the places where the Romanian national movement began. In May 1848 a great assembly of Romanians on its Field of Liberty demanded national rights.

Lope de Vega was a Spanish playwright and poet, one of the leading figures of the Spanish Golden Age. A prolific writer, he is said to have written some 1,500 plays, of which several hundred survive, including Fuenteovejuna and The Dog in the Manger. He shaped the Spanish comedia, the three-act play mixing tragedy and comedy that dominated the theatre of his time.

The Maitraka dynasty ruled western India from about 475 to 776 from their capital at Valabhi in Saurashtra, now Vala in Gujarat. Founded by Bhatarka, a general of the Gupta Empire, they became independent as Gupta power faded. Valabhi was a centre of Buddhist and Jain learning, where the Jain canon was written down at a council in the 5th century. The dynasty fell to Arab raids from Sindh.

The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World are a list of monuments drawn up by Greek writers of the Hellenistic period: the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. Only the Great Pyramid survives.

Langalibalele was chief of the Hlubi, a Nguni people of Natal, and was known as a rainmaker. In 1873 he refused to have the guns his men had earned at the diamond fields registered, and the Natal government treated this as rebellion, broke up the Hlubi location and exiled him to Robben Island. The affair caused controversy in Britain, and he was allowed to return to Natal in 1887.

Patwon Ki Haveli is a group of five adjoining merchant mansions in Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, begun in 1805 by the wealthy trader Guman Chand Patwa for his sons. Built of yellow sandstone, the houses are known for their carved facades, balconies and painted interiors. They are among the finest examples of the havelis built by Jaisalmer's merchant families.

Malang is a city in the highlands of East Java, Indonesia, and the second-largest city in the province. The area holds some of the earliest remains of Javanese kingdoms, including the Dinoyo inscription of 760 and Candi Badut, and later lay in the centre of the Singhasari kingdom. Under Dutch rule it became a cool hill town and plantation centre.

Kidal is a town in north-eastern Mali, in the Adrar des Ifoghas mountains of the Sahara. It is the main centre of the Kel Adagh Tuareg and was founded as a French post in the early 20th century. Since independence it has been the centre of repeated Tuareg rebellions against the Malian state.

Bagyendanwa is the royal drum of the Kingdom of Ankole (Nkore) in south-western Uganda. In Ankole tradition it was inherited by Ruhinda, founder of the Hinda dynasty, when Chwezi rule dissolved, and it represented the kingship itself: it was kept in its own shrine, attended by its own keepers and given offerings. Possession of the drum was essential to a legitimate mugabe.

Perthshire is a historic county of central Scotland, stretching from the Highlands of Atholl and Breadalbane to the lowland valley of the Tay. It contains Scone, where Scottish kings were inaugurated, and the early church centre of Dunkeld, and in the Pictish period it was the core of the over-kingship that grew into the kingdom of Alba. Its county town is Perth.

Yariri was a regent of Carchemish in the early 8th century BCE, ruling for the young prince Kamani. His Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions, carved on sculpted reliefs at Carchemish, boast that his fame reached Egypt, Babylon and other lands and that he knew several scripts and languages. He is one of the best-known figures of Neo-Hittite Carchemish.

Bondoukou is a town in north-eastern Côte d'Ivoire near the border with Ghana. An old centre of Dyula Muslim traders on the route between the Akan goldfields and the middle Niger, it lay in the centre of the Abron Kingdom of Gyaman, whose kings held court nearby. It came under French rule at the end of the 19th century and is known for its many old mosques.

Surame is the site of the ruined first capital of the Kebbi kingdom, in Sokoto State, north-western Nigeria. It was built by Muhammadu Kanta in the early 16th century and enclosed by massive earthen and stone walls, and it remained the royal seat until the kings moved to Birnin Kebbi. The Surame cultural landscape is on Nigeria's tentative list for World Heritage status.

Mapungubwe Hill is a flat-topped sandstone hill in the Limpopo valley of northern South Africa, near the confluence with the Shashe. Around 1220 the ruling elite moved onto its summit, apart from commoners below, and royal graves there contained gold objects including the famous golden rhinoceros. The site, abandoned around 1290, is part of a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape.

Pura Taman Ayun is a royal Hindu temple at Mengwi in southern Bali, Indonesia, built as the state temple of the Mengwi kingdom. Surrounded by a broad moat, with tiered meru shrines, it expressed the rulers' authority over irrigation and fertility. Since 2012 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape of Bali's subak irrigation system.

County Westmeath is an inland county in the Irish midlands, in the province of Leinster, with Mullingar as its county town. It was created in 1543 from the western part of the Anglo-Norman lordship of Meath, itself formed from the early kingdom of Mide. Its lakes and the Hill of Uisneach were the centre of Clann Cholmáin power.

Igbo-Ukwu is a town in Anambra State, Nigeria, where excavations by Thurstan Shaw in 1959–64 uncovered elaborate bronze castings, glass beads and a burial of a high-status figure. Dated to the 9th and 10th centuries, the lost-wax bronzes are among the oldest and most intricate in West Africa, and the beads point to long-distance trade. The finds are often linked to the ritual culture of Nri.

Etosha Pan is a large salt pan in northern Namibia, about 120 km long, which fills with water only briefly after heavy rains. Ovambo peoples collected salt there and traded it widely. It lies in the centre of Etosha National Park, proclaimed as a game reserve in 1907, which is one of Africa's best-known wildlife reserves.

Kinyarwanda is the Bantu language of Rwanda, spoken by nearly the whole population and closely related to Kirundi of Burundi. In the precolonial kingdom it was shared by Hutu, Tutsi and Twa alike, and the royal court cultivated dynastic poetry and oral history in it. It is one of the official languages of Rwanda.

Stefan Uroš I was King of Serbia from 1243 to 1276. He built up the kingdom's economy by inviting Saxon miners, who opened the silver mine at Brskovo, and by encouraging trade with Ragusa. He founded the monastery of Sopoćani, and in 1276 he was deposed by his son Stefan Dragutin and ended his life as a monk.

Rajasinha I was king of Sitawaka in Sri Lanka from 1581 to 1593, son of Mayadunne. Known as a soldier, he conquered most of the west and the central highlands, including Kandy, and besieged the Portuguese in Colombo in 1587–1588 without success. His conversion to Shaivism estranged the Buddhist clergy, and his kingdom collapsed soon after his death.

David III Kuropalates was a Bagratid prince of Tao in south-western Georgia from the 960s until his death in 1001. He helped Emperor Basil II defeat the rebel Bardas Skleros in 979 and was rewarded with large territories, and he built churches such as Oshki. He adopted his kinsman Bagrat III, which made possible the unification of Georgia under one king.

Soqotri is a Modern South Arabian language spoken on Socotra and its neighbouring islands, part of Yemen. Like Mehri, it is a Semitic language distinct from Arabic that preserves features of the pre-Islamic languages of southern Arabia. It has no traditional written form and is known for its oral poetry.

John Ball was an English priest whose preaching on the equality of all people made him one of the leaders of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Excommunicated and imprisoned several times for sermons attacking the wealth of the Church and the lords, he was freed from Maidstone prison by the Kentish rebels and preached to them at Blackheath on the text 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'. After the revolt collapsed he was captured at Coventry and executed at St Albans on 15 July 1381.

The Battle of Valmy, fought on 20 September 1792 in Champagne in north-eastern France, halted the Prussian-led invasion that threatened revolutionary Paris. French armies under Dumouriez and Kellermann held their ground in an artillery duel, and the Duke of Brunswick's army soon withdrew. The next day the newly assembled National Convention abolished the monarchy; Goethe, who was with the Prussian army, later wrote that a new era in the history of the world began that day.

Leopold I, called the Illustrious, was the first Babenberg ruler of the eastern march of Bavaria that became Austria. Emperor Otto II gave him the march in 976, and he pushed its frontier east along the Danube against the Magyars, ruling from Melk. He was killed at Würzburg in 994, and his descendants ruled Austria until 1246.

The Kru are a West African people of the coast of south-eastern Liberia and south-western Côte d'Ivoire, speaking Kru languages. From the 18th century they became known as sailors and dock workers, serving on European ships along the West African coast and settling in ports as far as Freetown and Lagos. In Liberia they were among the indigenous peoples long excluded from power by the Americo-Liberian settler elite.

The Mixtecs, who call themselves Ñuu Savi, 'people of the rain', are an indigenous people of western Oaxaca and neighbouring parts of Guerrero and Puebla in Mexico. Before the Spanish conquest they lived in many small kingdoms such as Tilantongo and Tututepec, whose histories they recorded in painted screenfold books, and were known for gold work and turquoise mosaic. Many fell under Aztec rule in the 15th century. Mixtec languages are still widely spoken.

Esperanto is a constructed international language created by the Polish ophthalmologist L. L. Zamenhof and first published in 1887. Designed to be easy to learn, with regular grammar and a vocabulary drawn mainly from European languages, it aimed to promote understanding between peoples. It became the most widely spoken constructed language, with a worldwide movement and its own literature.

The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley is a glacial valley in south-eastern Andorra, covering almost a tenth of the country's territory. Inscribed in 2004 as Andorra's only UNESCO World Heritage Site, it preserves a cultural landscape of summer pastures, stone shepherds' huts, terraced fields, tracks and traces of iron smelting that shows how people used high-mountain resources over a thousand years. No road runs through it.

The Treaty of Aarau, concluded in August 1712, ended the Second War of Villmergen between the Protestant cantons of Zürich and Bern and the Catholic cantons. It gave Zürich and Bern control of the common lordships in the Aargau and primacy in governing the others, ended the Catholic predominance established in 1531 and secured parity between the two confessions in mixed areas.

Sir John Kerr was Governor-General of Australia from 1974 to 1977. On 11 November 1975, after the opposition-controlled Senate had blocked the government's budget, he dismissed the prime minister Gough Whitlam and appointed Malcolm Fraser as caretaker until an election. The dismissal, which had no precedent in Australia, provoked a constitutional crisis and remains controversial.

Beaune is a town in the Côte-d'Or department of Burgundy, eastern France, in the centre of the Côte d'Or wine country between Dijon and Chalon-sur-Saône. It was the seat of the ducal parlement in the Middle Ages and is known for the Hospices de Beaune, a hospital founded in 1443 by the chancellor Nicolas Rolin. It is the main trading centre of Burgundy wine.

The Croÿ Tapestry is a large tapestry made in 1554 by Peter Heymans for Duke Philip I of Pomerania. It shows Martin Luther preaching before the families of the dukes of Pomerania and the electors of Saxony, celebrating their marriage alliance and Protestant faith. It is named after Ernst Bogislaw von Croÿ, the last heir of the Griffin dynasty, who left it to the University of Greifswald.

Liutgard of Saxony was a daughter of Count Liudolf, founder of the Liudolfing dynasty, and his wife Oda, who founded the convent of Gandersheim. In the 870s she married the Carolingian king Louis the Younger of East Francia, a match that showed the rising standing of her family. Her brother Otto the Illustrious led the Saxons after 880, and his son Henry the Fowler became king in 919.

Otto the Illustrious was a Saxon count of the Liudolfing family who held a dominant position in Saxony and Thuringia from 880 until his death in 912. A son of Count Liudolf, he succeeded his brother Bruno, who was killed fighting the Vikings, and he is counted as Duke of Saxony. His son Henry the Fowler was elected king of East Francia in 919, beginning the Ottonian dynasty.

The Battle of Iwo Jima was fought from 19 February to 26 March 1945, when United States Marines captured the volcanic island of Iwo Jima from Japan in the Pacific War. The Japanese garrison of about 21,000 under General Kuribayashi Tadamichi fought from tunnels and almost all died; American casualties numbered some 26,000, including nearly 7,000 killed. The flag-raising on Mount Suribachi became a famous photograph.

The Tarikh al-Hind, also known as Al-Biruni's India, is a study of Indian religion, philosophy, literature, astronomy, geography and customs written in Arabic by the scholar al-Biruni around 1030, while he served the Ghaznavid court. It is based on Sanskrit sources and conversations with Indian scholars.

Munjong of Goryeo was king of Goryeo from 1046 to 1083, a thirty-seven-year reign often seen as the height of the dynasty. He refined its institutions, revised the stipend land system in 1076 and promoted Buddhism and Confucian learning. Relations with Song China were renewed, and his son Uicheon became one of the leading monks of the age.

The Aulikara dynasty ruled the region of Dashapura, modern Mandsaur in western Malwa, in the fifth and sixth centuries CE, at first as subordinates of the Gupta Empire. Its most famous king, Yashodharman, claimed victory over the Huna ruler Mihirakula around 528 and boasted in his Mandsaur pillar inscriptions of conquests across northern India. After him the dynasty disappears from the record.

North China is the region of China north of the Huai River and the Qinling Mountains, centred on the Yellow River basin and the North China Plain. Farmed mainly for wheat and millet, it was where the early Chinese states arose and long the seat of government. Its open northern frontier made it the target of steppe peoples, and dynasties of northern origin such as the Northern Wei, Liao, Jin and Yuan ruled it.

The Golden Gate was the main ceremonial entrance of medieval Kyiv, built under Yaroslav the Wise around 1037 as part of the city's new fortifications, with a church above its passage. It was badly damaged when the Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240 and later fell into ruin. The surviving remains were enclosed in a reconstruction in 1982. The Golden Gate of Vladimir was modelled on it.

Tristan und Isolde is an opera by Richard Wagner, composed between 1857 and 1859 on the medieval legend of the lovers Tristan and Isolde. It was first performed in Munich on 10 June 1865 under the patronage of Ludwig II of Bavaria. Its harmonic language, beginning with the famous "Tristan chord", greatly influenced later music.

The Gobelins Manufactory is a tapestry works in Paris, on the site of the dyeing workshops of the Gobelin family. In 1662 Colbert bought it for Louis XIV and made it a royal manufactory producing tapestries and furniture for the royal palaces under the painter Charles Le Brun. It became a model of state-sponsored luxury industry and still operates under the French state.
